title: Charess stands her ground: ‘cosplay is not consent’
summary: SEOUL, South Korea—Filipina cosplayer Charess is well-aware of the rising and alarming issue regarding the objectification of women in her own scene. As someone who has been in the limelight since…

blocks.text: SEOUL, South Korea—Filipina cosplayer Charess is well-aware of the rising and alarming issue regarding the objectification of women in her own scene.
As someone who has been in the limelight since 2017, Charess has seen the beauty of switching from one character to another. However, like Yin and Yang, she saw the ugly in it as well.

Charess has been cosplaying for over nine years, flaunting her famous personifications of characters from VALORANT, Monster Hunter and Honkai Impact, much to the delight of gamers and even casuals around the country.
In fact, she continued to boast her brilliance in Seoul, dressing up as Kai’Sa from League of Legends: Wild Rift for this year’s edition of SMASH.
She could have been thinking about how stunning her newest persona was, she could have been reveling in the praises of her newest cosplay.
Instead, she had to keep one eye open for rather rude comments from thirsty men on social media.
Fortunately for Charess, she knows her way around the distasteful remarks.

“Sometimes, I just talk to them directly in the comments, I answer them,” she revealed in an exclusive interview with TECH Inq. “Most of the time, I ignore them and block them because I feel like the more I give them attention, the more they do those kinds of things.”
The sad part about Charess’ sentiment is simple; women cosplaying shouldn’t be an issue.
According to the 26-year-old figure, women should be able to channel their favorite characters without having to worry about being catcalled or be recipients of repulsive remarks.
‘Shame on you’
Sadly, the most recent issue regarding a Pokémon TCG community and fellow cosplayer Een Mercado showed that wasn’t exactly the case.
A few weeks back, certain members of the community were called out after having their group chat messages leaked. Those messages showed multiple instances of inappropriate conduct.
Mercado was one of the women on the receiving end of the unpleasant comments.
“I saw all the remarks about me and it just shows how these men are. Regardless of when it was made, you guys should be shameful about yourselves,” said Mercado upon finding out about said comments.
“And you’re the very ones who keep saying that you do it for the community, yet this is how you treat people. Shame on you.”
Charess isn’t far off from Mercado’s situation.
The sad—and rather, awful—part about it is, even when Charess isn’t in her natural habitat of putting on a costume, she still receives misogynistic statements from randoms on the net.

“Even when I’m wearing a covered outfit, people will still objectify you and they always find a way to do that. But, I just learned to ignore everything and block so I don’t have to spend a lot of energy dealing with those.”

For cosplay, for women
Charess’ and Mercado’s latest barbs were directed towards offensive and unpalatable words for the cosplaying community.
Both women, who should feel safe inside and outside the scene, know it’s more than that now.
Their stands aren’t just for the cosplaying scene, they’re also for women everywhere. Both situations deserve one minute and simple value; respect.
“I would like everyone to know that cosplay is not consent. You guys [fellow cosplayers] should stand on what you believe in,” said Charess.
“You should not let other people treat you badly because everyone deserves to be treated with respect.”

The MNL Card Convention has since condemned the member of the community who made the distasteful remarks on Mercado and several other women. Not that he needs or even deserves to be named and given more attention than he already has.
That’s one step closer to both women’s bare minimum demand.
Maybe this time, it’s time for people outside the TCG community and the cosplay scene to take a stand like Charess and Mercado.
That stand shouldn’t be for the good of cosplaying alone. It should also be for the good of women around the country too.
